newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish prime minister may face no-confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Polish prime minister may face no-confidence vote.

text.p: The Peasant Party (PSL), junior partner in Poland's ruling leftist coalition, said on Tuesday it would seek the dismissal of Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, an ex-communist, over his agricultural policies.
The Peasants said Cimoszewicz had to go because he was delaying a decision to grant farmers advance payments for the 1997 grain harvest.
Other parties dismissed the demand as part of the PSL's campaign for September general elections.

"The prime minister continues to neglect problems of agriculture, which causes tension in the countryside and destabilises the food market," PSL spokesman Aleksander Bentkowski told a news conference.
The Peasants' parliamentary caucus will meet next Tuesday to draft a no-confidence motion against the prime minister, which parliament could vote on late in August, he said.

Cimoszewicz, from the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), and his spokewoman were not available for comment, but the ex-communists' leader Jozef Oleksy said his party continued to back the prime minister.
"We support Cimoszewicz. We think it is not right to present ultimatums in matters that concern the economy," Oleksy told reporters before meeting Cimoszewicz.

Finance Minister Marek Belka said the Peasants' proposals could cost the national budget up to 260 million zlotys ($75 million), more than it could bear, especially as it had been strained by costs of July's catastrophic floods, which killed 54 people.
Cimoszewicz said last week he needed more time and details before deciding on the best way to help the farmers, who often find it hard to sell grains after last year's large imports. @
The PSL's no-confidence motion, if filed, appeared to have little chance to succeed because the opposition had signalled it would not support the proposal.

"It is pointless to dismiss the prime minister just weeks before the elections. Voters will soon judge for themselves," Henryk Wujec, a senior official of the opposition Union for Freedom party, said late last week, when the PSL first suggested it might try to sack the premier.
The Peasants alone do not have a simple majority needed to oust Cimoszewicz but they could obstruct the workings of the government to press for his dismissal. @
The ex-communists brushed off the Peasants' threat as jockeying for electoral advantage before the polls, due on September 21, among rural voters.
"This is a political game aimed at creating an impression that the PSL is good for farmers while the SLD is bad," SLD spokesman Andrzej Urbanczyk told Reuters.

The opposition agreed. "This is aimed at creating a propaganda effect," said Tomasz Tywonek, spokesman for the Solidarty Election Action (AWS), seen as the main rival of the ex-communists at the ballot.

The ex-communists and the AWS are running neck-and-neck in public opinion polls with more than 20 percent of support. The Peasants, who joined the often uneasy government coalition in 1993, are trailing badly with about 10 percent.
